lesson.title: Discover or Relay: STUN and TURN
lesson.summary: STUN helps a host discover the public IP and port a NAT is presenting for it, enabling hole punching, while TURN falls back to relaying traffic through a third-party server whenever a direct connection still cannot be made.
lesson.body:
NAT traversal, as the previous chapter laid out, hinges on both peers knowing each other's actual public-facing address and port, not just their private, local address, which is meaningless outside their own network. STUN, short for Session Traversal Utilities for NAT, solves exactly that discovery problem. A STUN server is a small, publicly reachable service that does one simple thing: when a host sends it a request, the STUN server looks at the public IP address and port the request actually arrived from, since the NAT already rewrote it on the way out, and reports that back to the host in its reply. The host now knows what its own connection looks like from the outside, information it has no way to determine just by inspecting its own local network configuration, since the NAT is the one doing the rewriting. Two peers can each query STUN, exchange the public addresses they learned, typically through some other channel both can already reach, like a signaling server used only to introduce them, and then attempt the hole-punching technique described earlier using those addresses.

STUN only helps with discovery, it does not relay any of the actual application traffic, and it does not work in every situation. Some NATs, particularly symmetric NATs, assign a different public port for every distinct destination a host talks to. In that case, the port the STUN server observed only applies to traffic exchanged with the STUN server itself, it is not the port that will be used when the host later tries to talk to the actual peer, so hole punching using that address fails. There are also network setups, certain restrictive firewalls, for instance, where inbound peer-to-peer traffic is blocked outright no matter what address is used.

TURN, short for Traversal Using Relays around NAT, is the fallback for exactly these cases. Instead of trying to establish a direct path between the two peers, both peers connect outbound to a TURN server, which each can reach normally since it is just an ordinary outbound connection to a public server, and the TURN server relays traffic between them. Everything one peer sends gets forwarded by the TURN server to the other, and vice versa. This always works, because it never depends on either peer accepting an unsolicited inbound connection, but it comes at a real cost. All traffic now flows through a third-party server rather than directly between the peers, adding latency and consuming that server's bandwidth for the life of the connection, which is why it is used as a fallback rather than the default.

In practice, real-time applications like video calling typically try a direct, STUN-assisted connection first, since it is cheaper and lower latency, and only fall back to a TURN relay when direct connection attempts fail. The combined framework that tries the available options in order, direct connection, then STUN-assisted hole punching, then TURN relay as the last resort, is commonly called ICE, for Interactive Connectivity Establishment. STUN and TURN are the two building blocks it coordinates between, not competing alternatives to each other.
